summary: Extends Kerberos with a new authorization data type, AD-AUTHENTICATION-INDICATOR. It lets a service ticket carry a note about how strongly the client was authenticated, so services can use that note in access decisions. It updates RFC 4120.

eli5.summary: When you enter a building, your badge could show whether you proved who you are with a password or a fingerprint too. The guard can then decide which doors to open.

questions: how to tell authentication strength in kerberos tickets
how do kerberos services know authentication strength
subtitle: A Kerberos ticket field that tells services how strongly the client was authenticated.

tldr.problem: Kerberos supports weak and strong ways to authenticate, such as passwords, one-time password devices and public-key cryptography. Application services had no standard way to learn which strength was used.
tldr.mechanism: The Key Distribution Center (KDC) can add an authorization data element of ad-type 97, AD-AUTHENTICATION-INDICATOR, inside an AD-CAMMAC container. It holds a list of strings, each naming requirements that were met at initial authentication.
tldr.outcome: Services can use the indicators in policy decisions, provided they validate the AD-CAMMAC container first. The RFC updates RFC 4120 to assign the ad-type number.

today: RFC 8129 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2017. It updates RFC 4120, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Tickets Need an Authentication Indicator
sections.content:
Kerberos (RFC 4120) lets users and services interact securely over a network. Through its pre-authentication framework (RFC 6113) it supports password-based authentication, multi-factor authentication with one-time password devices, public-key cryptography and other schemes.

Those schemes can offer very different strengths of client authentication. An implementation may keep track of which strength was used and feed it into policy decisions. This document specifies a new authorization data type that conveys that information to application services. Its elements appear inside an AD-CAMMAC container (RFC 7751).
sections.eli5: There are easy ways and hard ways to prove who you are. This gives the ticket a small label saying which way you used.

sections.title: Where the Indicator Fits in a Ticket
sections.content:
The indicator is produced by the KDC, the party that checks the client at initial authentication, and it is read by application services. It travels as authorization data in a ticket: the KDC MAY include it in initial credentials and MAY copy it from a ticket-granting ticket into service tickets, so a service ticket can report how the client first proved its identity.

The element is wrapped in an AD-CAMMAC container, so the contents can be verified as originating from the KDC. Because KDCs and applications that do not implement the element MAY safely ignore it, adding it does not break existing deployments that never look at it.
sections.eli5: The security office stamps the label when you first walk in, and the sticker stays on your badge as you move between rooms.

sections.title: The AD-AUTHENTICATION-INDICATOR Type
sections.content:
The KDC MAY include authorization data of ad-type 97, wrapped in AD-CAMMAC, in initial credentials. It MAY copy the element from a ticket-granting ticket into service tickets. The ad-data field holds the DER encoding of this ASN.1 type:

AD-AUTHENTICATION-INDICATOR ::= SEQUENCE OF UTF8String

Each string is a short value showing that a particular set of requirements was met during the initial authentication. Strings are meant to be compared against known values, not to store structured data. Each one MUST be either:

  • a URI that references a Level of Assurance Profile (RFC 6711), or
  • a site-defined string whose meaning is set by the realm administrator, which MUST NOT contain a colon.

The elements MUST be included in an AD-CAMMAC container so their contents can be verified as coming from the KDC. Applications and KDCs that do not implement the element MAY safely ignore it.
sections.eli5: The label is a short list of words, like a sticker that says "showed ID" or "used a key card". Only the building's own security office is allowed to put the sticker on.

sections.title: Assigned Numbers
sections.content: This RFC updates RFC 4120 in two ways. It assigns ad-type number 97 to AD-AUTHENTICATION-INDICATOR in the table in Section 7.5.4 of that RFC. It also updates the table in Section 5.2.6 to map ad-type 97 to "DER encoding of AD-AUTHENTICATION-INDICATOR". The IANA Considerations section says the document needs no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: The number 97 is now officially reserved for this label in the Kerberos rulebook.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because the elements sit inside AD-CAMMAC, which supersedes AD-KDC-ISSUED, both application services and the KDC can verify them. KDC implementations MUST use AD-CAMMAC verifiers as described in RFC 7751 so an attacker cannot modify the indicators. Application servers MUST validate the container before making authorization decisions, and MUST NOT base decisions on indicators that appear outside an AD-CAMMAC container.

Multiple strings can make a decision ambiguous. The RFC advises always using indicators as a positive sign that requirements were met. Its example is a "without-password" indicator: a service might read it as stronger authentication, but it could also be inserted when no authentication occurred, such as anonymous PKINIT.

Services that evaluate site-defined indicators MUST consider the realm of original authentication, to avoid cross-realm collisions. Failing to do so can lead to invalid authorization decisions.
sections.eli5: A label is only trustworthy if it is sealed by the security office, so guards must check the seal. A guard also has to know which building a sticker came from, because two buildings might use the same words differently.
